title: Judges 6:33–40
context: Judges 6:33–40 tells how Midian and its allies gather in the valley of Jezreel, the LORD’s Spirit comes on Gideon, and tribes rally to his trumpet and messengers. Gideon then asks God twice for a sign with a fleece, first wet on dry ground and then dry on wet ground, and God grants both. The text does not commend or condemn Gideon’s request directly. Interpreters in both traditions caution against treating the fleece as a pattern for discerning God’s will, while they recognize God’s patience with a hesitant servant who already had God’s word.

verses.text: Then all the Midianites and the Amalekites and the children of the east assembled themselves together; and they passed over, and encamped in the valley of Jezreel.
verses.arminianNotes: Midian, Amalek and the eastern peoples gather, cross the Jordan, and camp in the valley of Jezreel. Arminian readers see the threat growing just after Gideon’s reform, which tests whether he and Israel will now trust the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the valley of Jezreel was fertile land, the enemy’s goal at harvest. Both traditions read the verse as setting the stage for the deliverance God has promised Gideon in 6:14–16.

verses.text: But the LORD’s Spirit came on Gideon, and he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered together to follow him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s Spirit comes on Gideon, he blows a trumpet, and Abiezer gathers to follow him. Arminians see the Spirit empowering a hesitant man to lead, with his own clan, who recently wanted him dead, now following him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The Hebrew can be read as the Spirit clothing Gideon. Both traditions see the Spirit’s coming as God’s equipping for a specific task, as with other judges (3:10; 11:29), and not as a statement about Gideon’s personal holiness.

verses.text: He sent messengers throughout all Manasseh, and they also were gathered together to follow him. He sent messengers to Asher, to Zebulun, and to Naphtali; and they came up to meet them.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon sends messengers through Manasseh, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, and they come to meet him. Arminian readers see the tribes responding to the call, in contrast with the tribes that held back in Deborah’s day (5:16–17).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God gathering the forces he will later reduce so that the victory is clearly his (7:2). Both traditions read the verse as showing the Spirit’s work in Gideon bearing fruit in the people’s response.

verses.text: Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken,
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon tells God, "If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken." Arminians note that Gideon admits God has already spoken, so the request that follows comes from weak faith rather than from lack of clear guidance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the phrase "as you have spoken," which shows that God’s word was clear. Both traditions read the fleece as a request for reassurance, not as discovering an unknown will, and they share a cautious view of it.

verses.text: behold, I will put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece only, and it is dry on all the ground, then I’ll know that you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon puts a fleece on the threshing floor and asks for dew on the fleece only, with dry ground. Arminian readers see God’s patience in allowing this request. Many Arminian teachers warn against using fleeces as a regular way to seek God’s will, since Scripture does not command it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise warn against making the fleece a pattern for guidance, and many compare it with Deuteronomy 6:16 against testing the LORD. Both traditions see the episode as describing what Gideon did, not prescribing what believers should do, and both see God’s kindness in answering.

verses.text: It was so; for he rose up early on the next day, and pressed the fleece together, and wrung the dew out of the fleece, a bowl full of water.
verses.arminianNotes: It happens as he asked: early the next morning he wrings out a bowl full of water from the fleece. Arminians see God answering Gideon’s weak faith generously, with a clear and abundant sign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note the detail of the full bowl, which makes the sign unmistakable. Both traditions read the verse as God’s condescending kindness toward a servant who was afraid, even though the sign was not strictly needed.

verses.text: Gideon said to God, “Don’t let your anger be kindled against me, and I will speak but this once. Please let me make a trial just this once with the fleece. Let it now be dry only on the fleece, and on all the ground let there be dew.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon asks God not to be angry and requests one more test, the fleece dry and the ground wet. Arminian readers see Gideon himself aware that he may be pressing God too far, and they see honesty and fear mixed in his request.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversed sign as ruling out a natural explanation, since a fleece normally holds dew. Both traditions treat the request with caution and focus on God’s patience rather than commending Gideon’s method.

verses.text: God did so that night; for it was dry on the fleece only, and there was dew on all the ground.
verses.arminianNotes: God does so that night: the fleece is dry and the ground is wet with dew. Arminians close the chapter by stressing God’s patience and his willingness to strengthen the faith of a servant he has called.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the chapter ending with God’s faithfulness rather than Gideon’s strength. Both traditions read the answered fleece as preparing Gideon for chapter 7, where God will make clear that the victory is his alone.
